edition.deck: France imposes curfews after unrest; Ukraine disputes US support; Danish parties face fresh tests.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise overnight developments and genuinely new angles. The French curfews and political reaction, disputed US support for Ukraine, and fresh Danish policy and political developments lead this edition. Returning stories are included only where this gather adds a substantive development.

content.headline: France imposes local curfews as unrest exposes political and economic strains
content.shortHeadline: France imposes curfews as unrest tests government
content.standfirst: Authorities have restricted movement and gatherings in parts of Paris and other cities after violent protests and looting. The government faces questions over security failures, while France’s debt and political deadlock limit its room to respond.

image.caption: Emmanuel Macron addresses the nation after the unrest.

sources.originalTitle: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris
Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
Frankrigs økonomi er for stor til at redde, frygter verdenskendt økonom

segments.body: Overnight curfews were imposed in parts of central Paris and several other French cities after weekend riots and looting. Paris police set a 23:00–06:00 curfew for Place de la République and Les Halles; other cities announced partial restrictions on gatherings or movement.

segments.title: Security and political pressure
segments.body: Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged failures in anticipating the unrest and said police had lost control in some cities. The government says more than 2,500 people have been arrested; businesses and public buildings were damaged, and thousands of shops were affected.

segments.title: Limited room to respond
segments.body: The protests began with demands over schools and public services, then widened amid anger about living costs. The Guardian describes Macron as isolated after criticism from across the political spectrum; economist Paul Krugman warns France’s debt could pose a wider risk to the eurozone, while a Nykredit analysis cited by TV 2 says the situation remains manageable.

content.headline: Ukraine says US intelligence warnings remain unreliable as Trump pressures Zel ́
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine disputes US assurances as Trump turns up pressure
content.standfirst: A Ukrainian presidential adviser says warnings about Russian missile attacks remain incomplete, despite Washington’s denial of any change in intelligence sharing. Zelenskyy also says US arms deliveries are delayed, as Trump questions whether he should lead peace talks.

image.caption: A Ukrainian rescuer inspects the site of a deadly Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region.

sources.originalTitle: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv
Trump vil have en anden end Zelenskyj til at forhandle fred

segments.body: Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the BBC that US warnings about incoming Russian attacks remain inconsistent, sometimes arriving only moments before impact. The White House says intelligence sharing has not changed. Zelenskyy has also said a missile attack on Kyiv came with no warning, while a later attack had only minimal warning.

segments.title: Dispute extends to weapons and negotiations
segments.body: Zelenskyy told US senators that interceptor missiles paid for by European countries are awaiting approval from the US defence secretary, and said European transfers of Patriot missiles also need US consent. Washington says it is playing a constructive role in efforts to end the war; the missile delays and intelligence claims remain disputed.

segments.title: Pressure on Kyiv
segments.body: Trump said it may be time for someone else to negotiate for Ukraine and said he would discuss the war with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping whether or not Zelenskyy was present. DR’s US correspondent interprets the remarks as a further effort to pressure Zelenskyy; the Ukrainian side says it fears being excluded from decisions about its future.

content.headline: Albanian protesters keep up clashes as pressure mounts on prime minister
content.shortHeadline: Albanian protests enter seventh day of clashes
content.standfirst: Students and other demonstrators are demanding better university conditions and the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Authorities report 295 injuries, including 186 police officers, as the protests enter a seventh day.

sources.originalTitle: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police

segments.body: Protests in Albania have continued for a seventh consecutive day, with demonstrators clashing with riot police in Tirana. The movement, involving many high-school and university students, is driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.

segments.title: Disputed response
segments.body: Official figures cited by the BBC say 295 people had been injured before Monday’s violence, including 186 police officers. Human-rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani, who represents arrested protesters, says police often present little evidence in court; Rama has rejected negotiations with what he calls violence against the state.

content.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in suspected deliberate attack
content.shortHeadline: Australian MP critically injured after car strike
content.standfirst: Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta. Police have arrested a man and are investigating; the prime minister says the incident appears deliberate, but no motive has been confirmed.

image.caption: Helen Haines was taken to hospital after being struck outside her office in Wangaratta.

sources.originalTitle: 'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
Australsk politiker har kritiske skader efter muligt angreb
Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her life

segments.body: Helen Haines was critically injured after being struck by a car outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, Victoria. A 43-year-old man was arrested and a knife was seized from the vehicle. Police have not confirmed that the impact was deliberate, although Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described it as an apparent attack.

segments.title: Wider concern about threats
segments.body: Australian politicians say they have faced growing threats and some have changed how they meet constituents. Government figures cited by the BBC record 1,067 reports of harassing or threatening behaviour against senior officeholders in the year to June; the investigation into Haines’s case has not established a political motive.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that the attack should prompt a harder look at the normalisation of threats and abuse in politics, while stressing that the alleged attacker’s motive remains unknown.

content.headline: Israeli police detain 10 after attacks by settlers in occupied West Bank
content.shortHeadline: Israeli police detain 10 after West Bank settler attacks
content.standfirst: Police say the arrests follow attacks on a US photojournalist, European diplomats and Palestinians during the olive harvest. The journalist suffered serious injuries; rights groups say violence against Palestinians has often gone unpunished.

image.caption: Photojournalist Heidi Levine speaks to reporters from a hospital bed in Ramallah.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers

segments.body: Israeli police detained 10 people in a rare raid on settlers after weekend attacks in the occupied West Bank. US photojournalist Heidi Levine said masked men beat her while she covered the olive harvest, leaving her with serious injuries. A separate attack targeted European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives near Taybeh.

segments.title: Questions over enforcement
segments.body: Police said those detained were connected with attacks on foreigners and the construction of an illegal outpost; a court extended the detention of six men. Israeli rights group Yesh Din says it has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in three weeks, and argues that most investigations into such cases are closed without indictments.

content.headline: Japan launches mission to collect dust from Mars’s moon Phobos
content.shortHeadline: Mission launches to bring dust from Mars’s moon to Earth
content.standfirst: Japan’s MMX spacecraft is headed for Phobos, where it aims to collect about 10 grams of material and return it to Earth in 2031. Scientists hope the sample will help establish how Mars’s moons formed.

image.caption: The MMX spacecraft lifts off from Japan on its mission to Mars’s moon Phobos.

sources.originalTitle: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon

segments.body: A spacecraft launched from Japan on a mission to study Mars’s moons and collect a sample from Phobos. If successful, it will be the first sample returned from Mars or either of its moons. The spacecraft is due to reach Phobos in August 2027 and is expected to bring its sample back to Earth in 2031.

segments.title: A clue to the moons’ origins
segments.body: Scientists hope the sample will help distinguish between two explanations for Phobos and Deimos: that they formed from debris after an impact on Mars, or that they are asteroids captured by the planet. Researchers also hope the sample may contain grains from Mars itself.

content.headline: Rwandan critic Robert Kabera found beheaded in Uganda
content.shortHeadline: Rwandan government critic found beheaded in Uganda
content.standfirst: Former Rwandan army sergeant major Robert Kabera, a popular YouTuber and singer, was found dead outside Kampala. He had sought asylum in Uganda and criticised Rwanda’s president; the motive for the killing is not known.

image.caption: Robert Kabera was a popular YouTuber and singer.

sources.originalTitle: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded

segments.body: Robert Kabera, a former Rwandan army sergeant major who became a critic of President Paul Kagame, was found dead outside Uganda’s capital, Kampala. Ugandan police say his head has not been recovered. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution.

segments.title: Family fears
segments.body: Kabera had more than 144,000 subscribers to a YouTube channel that featured criticism of Kagame and his administration. His widow told the BBC she feared for the family’s safety. The Rwandan government has not publicly commented, and the circumstances and motive for the killing remain unclear.

content.headline: Trump uses France unrest to make immigration pitch to US voters
content.shortHeadline: Trump turns France unrest into a US election warning
content.standfirst: At a Kansas rally, Donald Trump portrayed France’s protests and looting as a warning about immigration and the US midterms. The demonstrations began over schools and living costs, before some turned violent.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Kansas.

sources.originalTitle: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France

segments.body: Donald Trump used unrest in France as a political argument at a rally in Kansas, blaming migrants and political opponents for the violence and telling voters to look at France ahead of the US midterms. He also urged France to close its borders, without evidence in the reporting to support his claim that migrants had taken over the country.

segments.title: What the protests are about
segments.body: The protests began with students’ demands over school conditions and widened to include concerns about fuel prices, purchasing power and public services. Some demonstrations were followed by looting and clashes with police; authorities have imposed partial curfews in several cities.

content.headline: Farage aide says £5m gift remarks were not Reform’s press office line
content.shortHeadline: Farage aide says £5m gift remarks broke party’s press line
content.standfirst: Undercover footage published by The Guardian shows Dan Jukes discussing Nigel Farage’s £5m gift and saying the Brexit-reward explanation was not the press office line. A parliamentary watchdog is investigating whether the money should have been declared.

image.caption: Dan Jukes discusses Nigel Farage’s £5m gift in undercover footage.

sources.originalTitle: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says

segments.body: Undercover footage published by The Guardian shows Dan Jukes, a former close aide to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, saying Farage’s description of a £5m gift as a reward for Brexit was “not the line to take from the press office”. Farage has also said the gift was for his security.

segments.title: Questions remain
segments.body: A parliamentary watchdog is investigating whether the gift from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne should have been declared. Harborne’s lawyers say it was unconditional and intended to support Farage’s security; the timing of the payments is disputed. Farage has not said how much, if any, was spent on security.

content.headline: Burnham asks officials to explore more radical options for Thames Water
content.shortHeadline: Burnham asks for new options to take control of Thames Water
content.standfirst: The prime minister has told officials to reconsider how to deal with the cash-strapped utility, including options that could involve public ownership and legal action. Thames Water has asked creditors for £2.4bn in additional funding.

image.caption: Ministers are considering converting some of Thames Water’s unpaid fines into a government stake.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water

segments.body: Andy Burnham has asked officials to develop new options for Thames Water, which is running short of cash, after previously promising to nationalise it. One proposal under discussion would convert about £100m of outstanding environmental fines into a government stake, giving ministers a say in the company’s running.

segments.title: Legal and financial obstacles
segments.body: Other options include placing Thames Water into a special administration process or stripping its licence, steps likely to face legal challenges. Government lawyers believe administration may be difficult while creditors keep the utility afloat and services continue. The company has asked creditors for an additional £2.4bn.

segments.title: Competing views
segments.body: Some advisers argue the government should move the company into special administration before it takes on more debt. Campaigners say a debt-for-equity arrangement would fall short of permanent public ownership; officials are also developing longer-term reforms to water-company ownership and bankruptcy rules.

content.headline: Tommy Robinson denies harassment charges as journalists’ trial opens
content.shortHeadline: Tommy Robinson denies harassing two journalists
content.standfirst: Prosecutors say Stephen Yaxley-Lennon shared images of two MailOnline journalists’ homes and encouraged followers to threaten them. He denies two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

image.caption: Tommy Robinson arrives at Southwark crown court for the start of his trial.

sources.originalTitle: Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told

segments.body: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denies two charges of harassment causing fear of violence against MailOnline journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. Prosecutors told Southwark crown court he circulated images of their homes to millions of followers and used social media and messages to target them.

segments.title: Evidence heard in court
segments.body: The prosecution says Dirnhuber and his partner left their home, while Young and his family were given close protection. The jury heard about posts, messages and a phone call in which Robinson allegedly said he would visit Young’s house. The case is ongoing; the allegations have not been proved.

content.headline: Russell Brand trial hears woman’s account of alleged rape at Soho bar
content.shortHeadline: Woman gives evidence in Russell Brand rape trial
content.standfirst: A complainant told jurors that Brand allegedly assaulted and raped her in 2004, and described waiting years before reporting it. Brand denies all seven charges; the trial continues.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at court on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape

segments.body: A woman told the jury at Russell Brand’s trial that he allegedly grabbed her at a Soho bar in 2004, pulled her into a toilet and raped her. In a police interview played in court, she said she closed her eyes and tried not to be present during the alleged attack. Brand has pleaded not guilty.

segments.title: The case continues
segments.body: Brand faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault relating to allegations from six women between 1999 and 2009. His barrister suggested the encounter was consensual; the complainant rejected that account. The trial is expected to last six weeks.

content.headline: UK MPs to debate higher compensation for families of workers killed by silicosis
content.shortHeadline: Parliament to consider higher payouts for silicosis families
content.standfirst: Draft regulations would increase compensation for relatives of people who die from industrial lung disease, including silicosis. If approved, the changes are due to take effect on 31 October.

image.caption: Sandra Elliott’s husband George died from silicosis after working with stone.

sources.originalTitle: Families of kitchen workers killed by toxic dust set to get thousands in compensation

segments.body: MPs are due to debate draft rules that would raise lump-sum compensation for families of workers who die from industrial lung diseases. Under the current scheme, bereaved families have received an average of £10,700, compared with £17,700 for living workers, according to The i Paper.

segments.title: The silicosis risk
segments.body: The proposed change follows campaigning over silicosis among workers cutting engineered-stone kitchen worktops, which can release fine silica dust. Almost 60 UK workers have been diagnosed so far, though doctors believe the true number may be higher. If Parliament approves the regulations, they are due to take effect on 31 October.

content.headline: Childcare support cap for larger families on universal credit to rise by April
content.shortHeadline: Childcare support cap for larger families to rise by April
content.standfirst: The government says the cap on childcare costs that larger families can claim through universal credit will increase before the end of the 2026–27 financial year. Campaigners say upfront payments and delays will still be barriers.

image.caption: The proposed change would raise the childcare support cap for larger families on universal credit.

sources.originalTitle: Parents on benefits to get £736 extra per child after lifting of cap by April

segments.body: The cap on childcare costs reimbursed through universal credit is due to rise by the end of the 2026–27 financial year, subject to legislative and delivery changes. The i Paper reports the change would add £736 for each additional child to the current monthly limit for families with two or more children.

segments.title: Upfront costs remain
segments.body: Parents can claim back 85% of eligible childcare costs, but must generally pay the fees first. Researchers and childcare groups say this can prevent people from taking up work or using the support, and point to delays and a sharp reduction in help when some families leave universal credit.

content.headline: Russia’s shadow fleet uses new tracking deception as vessels pass UK waters
content.shortHeadline: Russian tankers use new tricks to disguise their locations
content.standfirst: A new form of location spoofing makes some sanctioned Russian tankers appear in two places at once. Researchers and navigation experts warn that interference with tracking systems raises safety risks in crowded waters including the English Channel.

image.caption: A Russian-linked tanker passes through the Baltic region amid concern over shadow-fleet tracking tactics.

sources.originalTitle: Why Putin’s shadow fleet now poses greater danger to UK

segments.body: An analysis reported by The i Paper says at least a dozen Russian-linked shadow-fleet vessels have recently used a technique that makes a tanker appear at its true position and at a second, false location. The vessels carry oil that can help fund Russia’s war and are subject to sanctions.

segments.title: Safety and security concerns
segments.body: Automatic Identification System signals help nearby ships track one another’s position and course. Experts warn that manipulating the system could create navigation risks in busy waters. The report also cites concerns that some civilian vessels may be used for surveillance or other hostile activity; those risks are not evidence of a specific planned attack.

content.headline: New UK private parking code sets grace periods and limits some charges
content.shortHeadline: New parking code gives drivers time to leave or appeal
content.standfirst: A government code due to take effect on 21 December sets grace periods and requires some charges to be cancelled or reduced. Drivers will still need to appeal and show that a rule applies.

image.caption: The new code sets rules for charges at privately run car parks.

sources.originalTitle: The 10-minute parking rule that will see fines waived for drivers

segments.body: A new code for private car parks gives drivers five minutes to decide whether to stay and 10 minutes to leave after paid parking ends. It also provides for charges to be cancelled in some circumstances, such as a medical emergency or a faulty ticket machine, and caps some minor errors at £20.

segments.title: Drivers must appeal
segments.body: The rules are due to take effect on 21 December. They do not cancel tickets automatically: drivers must first appeal to the parking company, then may refer a rejected case to an independent service. The AA calls the code a good first step but says debt-collection fees remain a concern.

content.headline: Venstre’s crisis deepens ahead of Sunday meeting with party leadership
content.shortHeadline: Venstre faces a pivotal meeting after fresh internal split
content.standfirst: After Søren Gade quit parliament and five MPs opposed the party line on a nitrogen law, leader Troels Lund Poulsen will meet Venstre’s executive board on Sunday. The party is also polling at a historic low, according to DR.

image.caption: Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen is seeking support for the party’s direction.

sources.originalTitle: Det stormer i Venstre: På søndag venter et afgørende møde

segments.body: Venstre is preparing for an extraordinary executive-board meeting on Sunday after a period of internal conflict. Søren Gade has left parliament after disputes with the leadership, and five of the party’s 18 MPs voted against its line on a nitrogen law for agriculture.

segments.title: Direction and support
segments.body: Leader Troels Lund Poulsen has said the party must move away from its close ties to agriculture, but some members say its future direction is unclear. DR reports that Venstre recently polled at 5.8%, its lowest result in an Epinion poll for the broadcaster. The Sunday meeting is expected to give members a chance to raise concerns and assess support for the leadership.

content.headline: Vietnam state visit to Denmark brings trade ambitions and human-rights criticism
content.shortHeadline: Vietnam visit puts Danish trade and rights concerns in focus
content.standfirst: The Danish royal family is hosting Vietnam’s president, Tô Lâm, as the countries pursue closer trade ties. Critics point to repression of political opponents; Denmark’s foreign minister says individual rights remain a concern.

image.caption: The Danish royal couple welcome Vietnam’s president and his wife in Copenhagen.

sources.originalTitle: Dronning Mary bar nyt milliondyrt diadem til gallataffel
Kongeparret har besøg af leder fra "regime, der kan finde på nogle ret grimme ting"

segments.body: Vietnamese President Tô Lâm and his wife are on a three-day state visit to Denmark. King Frederik presented Tô Lâm with the Order of the Elephant, and the royal couple hosted a gala dinner. Danish companies including Lego, Carlsberg and Pandora have business interests in Vietnam.

segments.title: Rights and diplomacy
segments.body: Critics say Vietnam suppresses political opponents and cite the 2017 abduction of former official Trịnh Xuân Thanh in Berlin. Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said Denmark raised human rights with his Vietnamese counterpart, describing socio-economic rights as improving while individual rights remain challenged. He argued Denmark cannot limit dialogue to countries that meet its own standards.

content.headline: Danish minister proposes curbs on addictive algorithms after TikTok study
content.shortHeadline: Danish minister calls for ban on addictive social algorithms
content.standfirst: A Danish study found that test profiles could be recommended misogynistic content within minutes. A minister now wants a ban on addictive algorithms; researchers caution that exposure alone does not prove a change in young people’s views.

image.caption: Research minister Christina Egelund says she wants to curb addictive social-media algorithms.

source.credit: Foto: Ida Marie Odgaard / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Minister er rasende over kvindehad på Tiktok – vil forbyde algoritmer
Unge mænds feed flyder over med kvindefjendsk indhold: De eksponeres næsten dagligt
Særligt to interesser risikerer at trække unge mænd ind i manosfærens loop
Unge mænd møder kvindefjendsk indhold efter få minutters scrolling

segments.body: A Danish study found that fictional TikTok profiles modelling teenagers could encounter manosphere content after only a few minutes of scrolling; one profile was shown such material after 21 seconds. The researchers say their tests and small sample of young users cannot establish how exposure changes attitudes or represent all young men.

segments.title: Calls for platform rules
segments.body: Research minister Christina Egelund says she supports banning addictive algorithms and has also proposed an age limit of 15 for social media. The study’s findings have prompted concern from other officials and experts, while TikTok says it removes 98.1% of videos that breach its hate and hateful-conduct rules and is working to vary recommendations.

content.headline: Danish psychotherapy association admits some course marketing was misleading
content.shortHeadline: Psychotherapy association acknowledges misleading course claims
content.standfirst: Several private psychotherapy institutes advertised courses as equivalent to a master’s degree, but five of six applications for official level-7 recognition were rejected. The association says it should have been clearer about how courses were described.

image.caption: Kent Kristensen, a health-law lecturer at Aalborg University, criticised the course marketing.

sources.originalTitle: Dansk Psykoterapeutforening indrømmer 'vildledende' markedsføring

segments.body: Several institutes linked to the Danish Psychotherapists’ Association have described their courses as equivalent to master’s-level education. Danish authorities rejected five of six applications for official level assessment, according to documents obtained by DR; some institutes continued to use level-7 wording after the rejections.

segments.title: What the assessment means
segments.body: An official level assessment does not itself award a degree or grant credit, but it signals how a course compares with the formal education system. The association’s chair, Christina Lethien, acknowledged that its marketing had not been sufficiently precise. The association says private assessments are not official Danish level assessments or master’s degrees.

content.headline: Danish survey finds school costs strain low-income families
content.shortHeadline: Extra school costs put pressure on low-income families
content.standfirst: In an Epinion survey for Egmont, 54% of the lowest-income parents said school-related extra costs put pressure on family finances. One mother says class contributions and activities have forced her to cut her children’s Christmas-gift budget.

image.caption: Katja Franck, a mother of three, says school-related costs are difficult to manage.

sources.originalTitle: Katja må skære i børnenes julegavebudget for at kunne betale til klassekassen: 'Det er skamfuldt'

segments.body: More than half of the lowest-income parents surveyed said extra costs linked to public school put pressure on their household finances. The Epinion survey for Egmont found that 54% felt the strain. Katja Franck, a disability pensioner and mother of three, says she spent about 2,000 kroner on extra costs for her son’s class last year.

segments.title: Belonging as well as budgets
segments.body: Franck says she finds it difficult to tell other parents when a payment is unaffordable and has had to reduce her children’s Christmas-gift budget to cover a class contribution. The chair of Skole og Forældre says small costs can accumulate and that children may withdraw from activities when families are under financial pressure.

content.headline: Danish education minister starts school tour after weak PISA results
content.shortHeadline: Minister tours schools after weak PISA results
content.standfirst: Magnus Heunicke says he will visit schools to hear from teachers, leaders and pupils after poor results in the latest PISA assessment. He wants to expand a screen-free approach in younger classes, though the gather does not independently assess its effectiveness.

image.caption: Education Minister Magnus Heunicke visits Lille Næstved School.

sources.originalTitle: Efter elendig Pisa-måling tager Magnus Heunicke på skoleturné i hele Danmark

segments.body: Education Minister Magnus Heunicke has begun a tour of schools around Denmark following what he described as very poor results in the latest PISA study. He says he wants to speak with teachers, school leaders and pupils about what is working and what is not.

segments.title: Books and screens
segments.body: At his first stop, Lille Næstved School, Heunicke praised the use of books and writing in younger classes and said he wants to expand the screen-free approach. He argued it helps learning and concentration; the report presents this as the minister’s view, rather than an independently assessed result.

content.headline: Kolding fishing club floods after new pump sluice is reopened
content.shortHeadline: Kolding fishing club floods despite new flood defences
content.standfirst: A fishing club flooded about 15 minutes after a new pump sluice was reopened as water levels fell. The utility says the system worked as designed, but is open to reviewing when the sluice is opened.

sources.originalTitle: Enorm pumpesluse skulle holde byen tør – men efter 15 minutter var havnen oversvømmet

segments.body: A fishing club near Kolding harbour flooded on Sunday after water levels fell and a new pump sluice was reopened. The 125m-kroner installation had held back rising water from the harbour and town, but club member Morten Nielsen says water entered the building within about 15 minutes and trapped some people inside.

segments.title: Reviewing the threshold
segments.body: Bluekolding engineer Thomas Faarbæk said the sluice had worked as intended and that flooding at the low-lying club would have been worse without it. He said the utility could discuss how low the water should fall before the sluice is opened next time.

content.headline: What could happen during a prolonged power cut in Denmark
content.shortHeadline: How a prolonged power cut could disrupt everyday life
content.standfirst: A Danish risk-management lecturer outlines how a long blackout could disrupt mobile networks, water, healthcare, fuel and payments. The advice is about a potential scenario, not a report of a current outage.

sources.originalTitle: Du bruger det til (næsten) alt - men hvad sker der, hvis strømmen forsvinder i flere dage?

segments.body: A prolonged power cut could affect far more than lighting and heating, risk-management lecturer Lene Sandberg told DR. Mobile networks rely on powered masts, while fuel pumps, digital payment systems and many pharmacy services may also be disrupted.

segments.title: Preparing for knock-on effects
segments.body: Sandberg says water and wastewater systems may be affected because pumps need electricity, and that FM radio could be an important channel for official information if mobile networks fail. The Danish Emergency Management Agency recommends storing three litres of water per person per day for three days.

content.headline: Maddison marks his return as Tottenham claim first league win
content.shortHeadline: Maddison sparks Spurs’ first league win
content.standfirst: James Maddison scored on his first start in 18 months as Tottenham beat Coventry 3-1, moving off the bottom of the table. Dejan Kulusevski also returned after a lengthy injury absence.

image.caption: Tottenham beat Coventry 3-1 for their first league win of the season.

sources.originalTitle: Maddison's magic moment for Spurs - 18 months in the making

segments.body: Maddison made his first start since April 2025 and opened the scoring with a curling finish from 20 yards. Jack Rudoni equalised for Coventry before Omar Marmoush put Spurs back in front; Ben Davies added a late third after a goalkeeping error. It was Tottenham’s first Premier League win of the season.

segments.title: A welcome return, not a complete recovery
segments.body: Maddison missed most of last season with an ACL injury and then fractured his shoulder on the opening weekend of this campaign. Dejan Kulusevski came on late for his first appearance in 526 days. The win brought relief, but the report cautions that Spurs’ recent record remains poor and that one victory does not settle their wider problems.

content.headline: Ronaldo suspended by Portugal but will miss no international matches
content.shortHeadline: Ronaldo ban takes effect with no Portugal games missed
content.standfirst: Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 30 days and fined 255 euros after leaving Portugal’s camp in September. Because the ban was backdated, he has already served 19 days and will miss no Portugal matches.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 appearances for Portugal.

sources.originalTitle: Ronaldo given 30-day suspension and £215 fine by Portuguese FA

segments.body: The Portuguese Football Federation imposed the suspension after Ronaldo left the national team camp following a Nations League match in which he was an unused substitute, and after learning he would not start against Denmark. The federation said it considered his remorse and his contributions to the game; the fine is 255 euros (£215).

Ronaldo said coach Jorge Jesus had twice broken his word and described it as a breach of trust. Jesus denied making an agreement with him but has left open the possibility of a return. The ban runs from the Denmark match, so it will not rule Ronaldo out of Portugal’s next games.

content.headline: Palace boss Sage under pressure after Brighton thrashing
content.shortHeadline: Sage’s Palace future in doubt after 5-0 defeat
content.standfirst: Crystal Palace are reviewing a poor start under Pierre Sage after Sunday’s 5-0 loss to Brighton. The manager is under pressure, though the reporting also points to injuries, squad departures and financial limits.

image.caption: Pierre Sage joined Crystal Palace on a three-year deal in June.

sources.originalTitle: Palace manager Sage facing fight to keep his job

segments.body: Sage has won two of his first seven league games, and Palace have conceded 17 goals—the most in the division. The report says he is facing a fight to keep his job, but that he will be given more time for now. Further poor results could force chairman Steve Parish to decide whether to act.

segments.title: A defensive problem with several causes
segments.body: Palace’s recent defensive stability has been disrupted by the departures of key players and injuries. The club’s recruitment options have also been constrained by difficulty complying with Uefa financial rules. But the report says figures inside the club see Sage’s system and approach as part of the defensive problems, so the pressure is not explained by squad issues alone.

content.headline: Haaland a doubt for Manchester City as Semenyo faces eight weeks out
content.shortHeadline: Haaland doubtful as City lose Semenyo for eight weeks
content.standfirst: Erling Haaland is a doubt for Manchester City’s Champions League match after taking a knock to his foot. Antoine Semenyo is expected to be out for about eight weeks, leaving Enzo Maresca to weigh his forward options.

image.caption: Erling Haaland has scored eight league goals for Manchester City this season.

sources.originalTitle: Haaland a doubt, Semenyo out - what are Man City's options?

segments.body: Haaland scored twice against Ipswich on Saturday but was absent from the portion of Monday’s training session open to the media. Maresca said the striker would be assessed after training and could still be available. City are seeking a response after losing 4-2 to Paris St-Germain in their previous Champions League match.

segments.title: Options if Haaland cannot play
segments.body: Semenyo’s left knee injury is expected to keep him out for around eight weeks, ruling out one possible alternative at centre-forward. Maresca said Phil Foden could play in the position, while also noting that City do not have a natural replacement for Haaland in the squad. Haaland’s availability remains uncertain.

content.headline: Wiegman’s next task: refresh England while sustaining the Lionesses’ success
content.shortHeadline: Wiegman faces the challenge of rebuilding England’s core
content.standfirst: After extending her England contract through to after Euro 2029, Sarina Wiegman faces the task of renewing a successful team. The analysis also asks whether the game’s growing expectations can be sustained.

image.caption: Sarina Wiegman has won three European Championships, including two with England.

sources.originalTitle: Building Lionesses 2.0 - Wiegman's new challenge awaits

segments.body: Wiegman has won three European Championships, including two with England, and led the Lionesses to a World Cup final. But seven players who started the Euro 2022 final also started against Spain this year, when England lost 4-0. The team now need to develop successors while continuing to compete at the top level.

segments.title: A wider challenge for the women’s game
segments.body: Wiegman has given 24 players their England debuts, though only three have become established starters. The report notes that homegrown starters in the Women’s Super League have been declining as more overseas players arrive, while recent attendance figures suggest interest may have plateaued. Continued England success matters, but the analysis does not treat future crowds or trophies as guaranteed.

content.headline: Brighton’s fast start raises title talk, but sustainability is the test
content.shortHeadline: Brighton’s title talk meets the test of a long season
content.standfirst: Brighton have won four straight league games and scored 15 goals without conceding across them. Their attack and defence are drawing title talk, but the report stresses that sustaining the pace is another matter.

image.caption: Dion Dublin says Brighton’s start has been breathtaking and asks: “Why not?”

sources.originalTitle: Are free-scoring Brighton genuine title contenders?

segments.body: After seven matches, Brighton sit third with 16 points, behind Arsenal and Manchester City. They have scored more goals and conceded fewer than any other Premier League side so far, with 11 different league scorers. Match of the Day pundit Dion Dublin called them a frightening team, while a supporters’ podcast co-host said it was too early to call them title contenders.

segments.title: Depth and time will matter
segments.body: The report highlights Brighton’s recruitment and the contribution of young forward Charalampos Kostoulas, but also points to the challenge of juggling Conference League matches. It notes that most teams to score at least 23 goals after seven Premier League games have finished in the top three, while Newcastle’s 1994-95 side is a warning that a brilliant start is no guarantee of a lasting challenge.

content.headline: How Canada closed the gap on England’s unbeaten Red Roses
content.shortHeadline: Canada’s rise ends England’s long unbeaten run
content.standfirst: Canada’s 24-21 win ended England’s 41-match unbeaten run, but the analysis finds more than a one-off upset: Canadian players have gained experience in England, while the Red Roses have had to manage absences and a changing motivation.

image.caption: Canada’s late fightback ended England’s unbeaten run.

sources.originalTitle: How have Canada closed gap to world champions England?

segments.body: Canada had lost all seven of their meetings with England this decade before a draw in September and Friday’s three-point win in Toronto. The report says Canada can reach a high level despite being less consistent, and points to head coach Kevin Rouet and several players gaining experience in England’s professional league.

segments.title: England’s response
segments.body: England were without regular captain Zoe Stratford, second rows Abbie Ward and Rosie Galligan, back-rower Marlie Packer and retired wing Abby Dow. The report also raises the psychological challenge of finding new goals after years of dominance and a home World Cup triumph. Amy Cokayne said England did not need to throw out their approach, while acknowledging the defeat.

content.headline: The ODI rule change bringing reverse swing back into focus
content.shortHeadline: How one ODI rule change is boosting late swing
content.standfirst: Since July 2025, captains have been able to choose which ball is used for the final 16 overs of an ODI. The older ball is swinging more, making death bowling harder to hit and changing how teams plan their innings.

image.caption: England are returning to ODI cricket after the rule change brought reverse swing back into focus.

sources.originalTitle: How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricket

segments.body: The change lets a captain select one of the two white balls after 34 overs, so it can become older and rougher before the innings ends. Since the rule was introduced, half of pace bowlers’ full deliveries in the final 10 overs have swung by more than one degree, compared with 35% before. Pace bowlers’ economy rate in the final five overs has also fallen.

segments.title: The impact varies by conditions
segments.body: England’s death-overs bowling numbers have improved markedly, although the report cautions that the team’s broader progress makes it difficult to attribute the gains to the rule alone. The effect has been strongest in England; there is less evidence from South Africa, where few ODIs have been played under the new conditions. Teams may need to score more of their runs earlier if late movement increases there.

content.headline: Michael Kiwanuka’s Fudge is rough-edged, lush and full of life
content.shortHeadline: Michael Kiwanuka’s Fudge finds life in the rough edges
content.standfirst: Recorded alongside Small Changes but made in a different spirit, Kiwanuka’s delayed album is a vivid, melodic work in its own right. Its reflections on musical uncertainty resonate differently after his stroke.

image.caption: Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.

sources.originalTitle: Michael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody

segments.body: Fudge began as a set of jams recorded alongside Michael Kiwanuka’s 2024 album Small Changes, but it sounds less polished and more immediate. Tape hiss, abrupt starts and extended playing give it a live-in-the-studio feel, while lush strings and memorable melodies make the songs feel carefully shaped rather than rough for roughness’ sake.

segments.title: A different resonance
segments.body: Kiwanuka’s release was delayed after he had a stroke and spent months in hospital; he said he was putting the record out because he did not know how long it would be before he could release another. Songs that dwell on his future in music now carry an added weight, though the review hears an artist who sounds sure of what he wants to do.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall album turns a live night into something lasting
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter makes a live night feel like a new beginning
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo recording pares his songs back to voice and piano, revealing new qualities in familiar material and introducing three unreleased songs from a career-making performance.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: On Live at Carnegie Hall, Cameron Winter reshapes songs from Heavy Metal with just his voice and piano. The review hears the spaces between notes opening up, turning one song that once moved with a small, plodding click track into something that glides. Three unreleased songs from the concert add to the sense of an evening with its own momentum.

segments.title: A performance becoming a record
segments.body: The album and its accompanying concert film preserve Winter’s December 2025 Carnegie Hall performance, where filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson and Benny Safdie appeared onstage with a camera. The review sees the recording as more than a document: the songs seem to outgrow the circumstances of their creation and take on the stature of standards.

content.headline: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album finds a sharp voice in romantic chaos
content.shortHeadline: Rachel Chinouriri makes emotional messiness feel like pop
content.standfirst: On i think i spoke too soon, Chinouriri’s conversational songwriting meets a shinier sound. The review finds her most compelling when goofy romantic drama and genuine vulnerability occupy the same song.

sources.originalTitle: I think I spoke too soon

segments.body: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album is her most polished, pairing her familiar alt-rock and pop instincts with brighter, more synth-heavy production. The smoother sound sometimes competes with her voice, but the review says the record finds its stride when arcade-like details and guitars frame her funny, unsettled account of young love.

segments.title: The charm of the contradiction
segments.body: Songs such as “I’m a star” and “AAAHHH!!!” let Chinouriri play up the drama without losing the feeling underneath it. The review argues that her emotional instincts make her more than another relatable pop persona: her insecurity and self-awareness sound convincing whether she is joking or letting the hurt show.

content.headline: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II turns a shoegaze band’s network into a mixtape
content.shortHeadline: TAGABOW’s mixtape opens up its wide-ranging musical world
content.standfirst: They Are Gutting a Body of Water bring more than a dozen collaborators into a 29-track set that moves between shoegaze, footwork, folk and rap, while also showcasing the Philadelphia label Julia’s War.

sources.originalTitle: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II

segments.body: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II takes its mixtape logic seriously: the 29 tracks draw in artists from the Julia’s War roster and beyond, with the sound shifting from Hotline TNT’s sustained guitars to a footwork collaboration with DJ Manny and laid-back rap over emo-tinged loops. The review hears a band widening its palette without losing its own identity.

segments.title: A community in the music
segments.body: The compilation also connects the label’s emerging artists with better-known collaborators. Greg Mendez’s folk melodies swell into distortion, while Horse Jumper of Love’s slowcore is pushed into a more urgent register. Rather than hiding behind a compilation, the review suggests, TAGABOW stand alongside artists they admire and invite listeners into their wider musical community.

content.headline: Worldpeace DMT make playful, carefully built pop on Stick Around for Tea
content.shortHeadline: Worldpeace DMT find feeling beneath their playful pop
content.standfirst: Leo Fincham and Rowan Please scale back the sampling sprawl of their debut for songs that play with the tension between childhood and adulthood, irony and earnestness.

sources.originalTitle: Stick Around for Tea

segments.body: Stick Around for Tea finds Worldpeace DMT making more room for songs than for the collage of sounds on their debut. Their finely assembled pop combines slinky strings, stray rattles and electronic textures, with Rowan Please’s playful delivery and Leo Fincham’s synthetic, sometimes bass-like voice pulling in different directions.

segments.title: Is the joke sincere?
segments.body: The album’s schoolroom theatricality invites listeners to wonder whether the duo mean what they sing. The review argues that the question is part of the point: childlike playfulness and adult understanding meet in songs that can sound like nursery rhymes one moment and finely wrought expressions of longing the next.

content.headline: Jess Williamson’s A Mile South of Heaven finds her at home in country
content.shortHeadline: Jess Williamson turns distance into intimate country songs
content.standfirst: Produced by Shooter Jennings, Williamson’s sixth album works through her ties to Texas and Los Angeles without forcing a choice between them. The review hears her most assured songwriting yet.

sources.originalTitle: A Mile South of Heaven

segments.body: On A Mile South of Heaven, Jess Williamson moves further into country, with pedal steel, fiddles and a natural Texas twang replacing much of the indie-rock sheen of earlier work. The songs keep returning to the distance between Texas and Los Angeles, making each place a source of longing as well as a place to leave.

segments.title: A voice that carries history
segments.body: The review praises Williamson’s phrasing and songwriting for making small details feel lived-in. In songs such as “Country Mile” and “The Gem and Mineral Show”, the narrator’s perspective shifts, turning familiar country themes of restlessness into a more searching account of becoming oneself and facing what follows you.

content.headline: You Can See Everything turns Elizabeth Holmes into an unsettling mystery
content.shortHeadline: Elizabeth Holmes remains an enigma in You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary has earned strikingly strong reviews, but its close access to Holmes does not settle the question of how she understands her own fraud conviction.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose in 2022.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster
The reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever?

segments.body: The documentary follows Elizabeth Holmes, her partner and their young children in the weeks before she reported to prison for defrauding investors in Theranos. She insists that she never lied and that the company’s blood-testing device worked; the film juxtaposes her account with Nathan Fielder’s visible scepticism and, later, another voice that questions whether he may be too caught up in her story.

segments.title: Acclaim, without a verdict
segments.body: The Guardian report notes the film’s exceptional early review scores and box-office opening in the US and Canada. The BBC account, drawing on the filmmakers’ festival remarks, describes a documentary that leaves competing explanations open: Holmes may be deliberately manipulative, or she may genuinely believe her own claims. Neither account presents that puzzle as resolved.

content.headline: A 1972 Harlem reunion brings Renaissance artists back into the room
content.shortHeadline: A Harlem Renaissance reunion, rediscovered on film
content.standfirst: Once Upon a Time in Harlem restores footage of a 1972 gathering of writers, artists and musicians who helped shape the Harlem Renaissance. Their lively disagreements become part of the film’s record of a movement and its legacy.

image.caption: Guests at the Harlem Renaissance reunion filmed for Once Upon a Time in Harlem.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunion

segments.body: Filmmaker William Greaves invited surviving figures of the Harlem Renaissance to a 1972 gathering at the Duke Ellington House and filmed their conversations. His granddaughter Liani Greaves and son David have shaped the material into a 100-minute documentary, restoring footage from a much larger archive and keeping the focus on the party and its guests.

segments.title: A movement, not a monolith
segments.body: The guests remember their work and argue over how the Renaissance should be understood. Romare Bearden challenges historian Nathan Huggins over the place of visual artists in his account, while the presence of George Schuyler draws visible disapproval. The filmmakers see those differences as evidence of a community with shared ambitions, not a single point of view.

content.headline: Fatherland finds Thomas Mann caught between postwar Germany’s divides
content.shortHeadline: Fatherland puts Sandra Hüller at the heart of a family crisis
content.standfirst: Paweł Pawlikowski’s restrained monochrome drama follows Thomas Mann’s 1949 return to Germany, where public recognition cannot quiet private grief or resolve the political ambiguity of his homecoming.

image.caption: Sandra Hüller as Erika Mann and Hanns Zischler as Thomas Mann in Fatherland.

sources.originalTitle: Fatherland review – Sandra Hüller brings a bayonet of intelligence to Paweł Pawlikowski’s taut return

segments.body: Thomas Mann returns from exile to a divided Germany, accepting honours in both Frankfurt and the communist East German city of Weimar. As he tries to stand above the political divisions, his daughter Erika, played by Sandra Hüller, grieves for her brother Klaus and challenges the cost of her father’s distance.

segments.title: The cost of standing apart
segments.body: The review sees the family story as inseparable from Mann’s public choices. His attempt to avoid taking sides is unsettled by Klaus’s writing and by the news that reaches the family during the tour. Pawlikowski’s controlled, monochrome film offers little consolation, framing survival and cultural belonging as questions rather than answers.

content.headline: The Night Is Fading Away turns a cinema into a refuge in Argentina
content.shortHeadline: A cinema becomes a refuge in The Night Is Fading Away
content.standfirst: After budget cuts push a projectionist into a night-watchman role, a single-screen cinema becomes a home for people on the margins. The film connects their shared refuge to political action in the wake of Javier Milei’s election.

image.caption: Pelu, played by Octavio Bertone, in The Night Is Fading Away.

sources.originalTitle: The Night Is Fading Away review – hypnotic homage to cinema as a force for public good

segments.body: Set in Córdoba, Argentina, The Night Is Fading Away follows Pelu, a cinema projectionist reassigned as a night watchman after city budget cuts. He leaves his cramped rental and secretly lives at the theatre, where he welcomes an unemployed roommate, an ageing drifter and a sex worker who streams her shows from the building.

segments.title: Cinephilia beyond the screen
segments.body: The group watch films by directors including Jean Renoir, Yasujiro Ozu and Robert Bresson, but the review says their love of cinema is not simply a retreat into nostalgia. In the political climate after Milei’s 2023 election, the characters’ acts of vandalism turn the commercial space into a commune and a basis for action.

content.headline: Ben Affleck’s account reopens the story of Justice League’s troubled handover
content.shortHeadline: Ben Affleck’s remarks reopen Justice League’s history
content.standfirst: Affleck says Warner Bros used Zack Snyder’s family tragedy as an excuse to replace him on Justice League. The claim adds a new and serious dimension to a franchise story long framed around competing cuts and studio choices.

image.caption: Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.

sources.originalTitle: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all

segments.body: Ben Affleck has described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career and criticised the circumstances of Zack Snyder’s departure after his daughter’s death. Affleck alleged the studio used the family tragedy to justify replacing Snyder; the account is attributed to his interview on the Happy Sad Confused podcast.

segments.title: A franchise at a crossroads
segments.body: The commentary places Affleck’s allegation against the film’s already turbulent history, including Joss Whedon’s reshoots, Ray Fisher’s allegations of abusive conduct and Gal Gadot’s claim that Whedon threatened her career. Whedon denied the allegations. The piece argues that the handover may have weakened DC’s shared-film ambitions, while acknowledging that a Snyder-led alternative was no guarantee of success.

content.headline: Vampire Carnival has striking style but little beneath its love triangle
content.shortHeadline: Vampire Carnival’s atmosphere outpaces its story
content.standfirst: A grieving young woman is drawn into the world of a vampire carnival, where two performers compete for her attention. The review enjoys the film’s visual flair but finds its characters and conflicts underdeveloped.

image.caption: Pauline Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire Carnival.

sources.originalTitle: Vampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of war

segments.body: Gemma visits a carnival with her friends and discovers that its performers are vampires who follow a rule against killing without consent. Two men, the gentle Sebastian and her estranged ex Eric, pull her into a love triangle. The review praises the directors’ visual set pieces, including a tracking shot through the fair and a confrontation in a hall of mirrors.

segments.title: A conflict left in the shadows
segments.body: The film’s mood and good looks do not fully compensate for a story that shifts between treating Eric as a tragic figure and a dangerous loose cannon. The review finds the disagreement over vampire conduct underexplored and says the backstories do not prepare the ground for the ending.

content.headline: Fourteen film flops that deserve another look
content.shortHeadline: From The Thing to Babylon: 14 flops worth revisiting
content.standfirst: A list prompted by Digger’s poor box office makes the case for films whose reputations changed with time, from The Thing and Dune to Dredd and Babylon.

image.caption: Films that flopped on release but later found admirers.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The collection ranges from films that were misunderstood on release to ambitious projects whose failures became part of their legend. The Thing arrived amid a turn towards feel-good blockbusters; David Lynch’s Dune was shaped by a director who later disowned it; and Last Action Hero’s self-aware humour looks less out of place in retrospect.

segments.title: Failure is not the final verdict
segments.body: Other picks include Heaven’s Gate, Cloud Atlas, Dredd and Babylon: films whose unevenness or commercial disappointment does not erase their visual ambition or pleasures. The list uses Digger as a starting point for a broader reminder that box-office performance and later cultural standing do not always match.

content.headline: Galaxy Quest makes a warm-hearted case for taking fandom seriously
content.shortHeadline: Galaxy Quest finds kindness in its science-fiction parody
content.standfirst: The 1999 comedy sends a cast of washed-up television actors into a real interstellar crisis. Its affectionate jokes about fandom give way to a story about commitment, community and the power of make-believe.

image.caption: The cast of Galaxy Quest, including Tim Allen, Alan Rickman and Sigourney Weaver.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movie

segments.body: In Galaxy Quest, aliens mistake a cancelled science-fiction show for historical fact and enlist its actors to help them. The film plays with genre conventions and television’s old-fashioned effects, but the essay argues that its affection for the fans is just as important as its parody.

segments.title: The joke is never on the fans
segments.body: The Thermians’ earnest belief in the show forces the actors to take their roles seriously, while a young fan helps save the day. The essay sees that as the film’s kindest idea: stories can matter to people even when outsiders think the costumes, lore or performances are silly.

content.headline: How Come Dine With Me made dinner-party awkwardness great television
content.shortHeadline: The people, not the food, made Come Dine With Me
content.standfirst: The show’s creator and narrator recall how a badly cooked dinner inspired a long-running format. Their account reveals the show’s carefully maintained balance between affectionate teasing and humiliation.

image.caption: A moment from Come Dine With Me.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Someone served sushi off a guy’s naked chest!’ How we made Come Dine With Me

segments.body: Come Dine With Me began after an executive producer’s disastrous attempt at a dinner party. The idea grew into a competition in which strangers take turns hosting, but Channel 4’s insistence that contestants be competent cooks helped shape the eventual format. A name change, a more conversational narrator and a focus on the guests made it something different from a straightforward food contest.

segments.title: The joke has a boundary
segments.body: The creator says the programme aims to puncture pomposity without sneering at contestants. Dave Lamb describes using the same principle for his voiceover: he avoids saying something he would not say to a participant’s face. The show’s creator credits its longevity to the ordinary people around the table, while Lamb says its appeal lies in watching how people live and feed themselves.

content.headline: Sebastian Croft brings heartbreak and ambition to his first music EP
content.shortHeadline: Sebastian Croft moves from Traitors fame to songwriting
content.standfirst: The actor’s time on Celebrity Traitors introduced him to a wider audience, but his forthcoming EP is built from songs he has written since childhood and shaped by a painful first breakup.

image.caption: Sebastian Croft, actor and singer-songwriter.

sources.originalTitle: Celebrity Traitors’ Sebastian Croft: ‘It was scary – the first time I’m being me’

segments.body: Sebastian Croft says Celebrity Traitors was the first time he felt he was appearing as himself rather than playing a character. The actor, known for roles including Heartstopper and Game of Thrones, has also been writing songs since childhood; he says the forthcoming EP The Great Forever marks a long-delayed move into music.

segments.title: Songs from a difficult chapter
segments.body: Croft says his first serious breakup in 2023 became the catalyst for the EP, which he spent three years refining. Its songs turn uncertainty and hurt into indie pop, from the dream-pop of “Pretty People” to “Tokyo”, which condenses conflicted feeling into the line “F**k you, but I hope you’re alright.” He says he wants to pursue music all the way to headlining Glastonbury.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into the drama’s centre
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up makes a new family its centre
content.standfirst: The BBC drama relocates its family-law battles to Manchester and introduces a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creators and lead actor describe how the spin-off aims to widen representation while keeping the original’s appetite for relationship drama.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expecting to take over her father’s firm, until her mother’s death changes his succession plans. The series keeps the high-stakes divorce cases and family conflicts of The Split but centres a new family in Manchester, led by Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar.

segments.title: Representation in ordinary lives
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living everyday lives, rather than being defined by a narrow set of familiar plotlines. The series’ executive producer, Abi Morgan, says the spin-off retains the original’s focus on family and romantic turmoil while giving a new team room to shape its own version.

content.headline: Why The Celebrity Traitors is struggling to replace its early chaos
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors needs players willing to deceive
content.standfirst: An early Traitor’s dramatic mistake gave the series a thrilling opening, but a critic argues that subsequent contestants have been too cautious and media-trained to sustain the game’s central pleasures.

image.caption: Maya Jama in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: The Celebrity Traitors has lost its spark – and I know exactly why

segments.body: The review says the current series has lost momentum since Richard E Grant, newly made a Traitor, revealed his role almost immediately and was banished. It argues that the celebrity contestants’ awareness of their public images has made them reluctant to take the risks and play the villains that the format needs.

segments.title: Politeness versus play
segments.body: The critic points to Traitors James Acaster and Hannah Fry as examples of players who avoid bold deception, and contrasts their restraint with the mischief of the previous series’ winner, Alan Carr. This is a review’s assessment of the show’s performance so far, not a claim that the contestants have all approached the game in the same way.

content.headline: Gnomes finds fun in a town overrun by murderous garden ornaments
content.shortHeadline: Gnomes turns a garden-ornament apocalypse into fun
content.standfirst: A small-town police team faces a gnome-led killing spree in this six-part Australian horror-comedy. The review likes its pulpy energy and cast, even if the biggest mayhem takes time to arrive.

image.caption: Asa Butterfield in the horror-comedy series Gnomes.

sources.originalTitle: Gnomes review – Asa Butterfield takes on murderous garden ornaments in pulpy horror-comedy

segments.body: In Nompton, a festival awakens an ancient evil and murderous garden gnomes descend on the town. The police, already facing cuts, are unprepared for the crisis. The review praises the series’ knowingly pulpy tone, its dark-stormy-night opening and the mix of local officials, police officers and teenagers drawn into the action.

segments.title: A slow build with a playful payoff
segments.body: The review says the show takes a few episodes to reach its full mayhem, but finds the build entertaining and the cast well judged. Asa Butterfield gives his character the right degree of false confidence, while the direction and midnight-movie look keep the absurd premise lively.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani brings class and personal loss to new drama The Party
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party looks at class and ambition
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner adapted Elizabeth Day’s novel for television, drawing on her long interest in Britain’s class system. She also reflects on bereavement, creative rejection and how #MeToo changed her experience of film sets.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner of The Party.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: The Party centres on a birthday gathering where working-class journalist Martin and Tory politician Ben meet amid a secret and a clash of social worlds. Sarah Solemani plays Martin’s pregnant wife, Lucy, and says she initially tried to leave the role because she was also writing and running the series.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani says she has long struggled to get stories about British class made and was drawn to the novel’s character crossing those boundaries. She also recalls losing her mother at 16 and describes #MeToo as having dismantled parts of an old Hollywood system, including the conduct of dangerous men on sets.

content.headline: Ellie Taylor on hosting Strictly’s spin-off and adapting to change
content.shortHeadline: Ellie Taylor wants Strictly viewers to enjoy the change
content.standfirst: The comedian has taken over It Takes Two after auditioning for the main Strictly presenting job. She discusses viewer criticism, the appeal of leaning into the show’s camp humour and the demands of a packed presenting schedule.

image.caption: Ellie Taylor, presenter of It Takes Two.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie Taylor on the Strictly backlash: ‘People don’t like change’

segments.body: Ellie Taylor says hosting It Takes Two is a dream job, combining her enthusiasm for Strictly with years of stand-up and presenting. After viewers objected to a panel without professional dancers, she says the programme was already planning to bring them on and welcomed the audience’s engagement.

segments.title: The job she got
segments.body: Taylor auditioned for the main Saturday-night show but says she has made peace with not getting it. She argues that people can be resistant to change and urges viewers to focus on the dancing, while balancing the spin-off with a Radio 2 hosting role.

content.headline: Rainbow Six Tactics brings the shooter’s planning into turn-based play
content.shortHeadline: Rainbow Six Tactics turns preparation into the action
content.standfirst: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario and Rabbids to a tactical spin-off of Rainbow Six Siege. Its developers argue that careful preparation, rather than speed or brutality, makes the series a natural fit for turn-based strategy.

image.caption: A scene from Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics swaps the studio’s colourful Mario and Rabbids world for tactical operations built around the Rainbow Six series. In a hands-on demo set in Nigeria, a four-person team uses drones, explosives and coordinated movement to breach a guarded warehouse, retaining the tension of the real-time shooter in a turn-based structure.

segments.title: More than one way through
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequential decisions makes it well suited to tactics. Players can approach missions in different ways with 15 operators, and can arrest some enemies rather than kill them. The studio also describes the wider tactical-sim genre as niche but still active.

content.headline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse pairs gothic spectacle with demanding action
content.shortHeadline: Belmont’s Curse is thrilling, if uneven, vampire-hunting
content.standfirst: Rose Belmont fights to free Paris from demons in a new entry that prioritises fast, punishing combat over the series’ familiar exploration. The review finds real invention, though not every stretch of the adventure earns its place.

image.caption: Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.

sources.originalTitle: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

segments.body: Belmont’s Curse puts Rose Belmont, daughter of series regulars Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, in a demonic Paris. Its battles are frantic and demanding, with even minor enemies able to inflict heavy damage. The review finds the shift towards quick, skill-based combat a notable departure from earlier Castlevania games.

segments.title: A world of uneven challenges
segments.body: Exploration leans on difficult platforming rooms, traps and tools rather than the series’ usual emphasis on backtracking and secret-hunting. A castle library offers clever puzzles, but other areas rely on repetitive combat. The review says the game improves after Rose is forced to confront her family legacy, though it does not match the strongest of its contemporary peers.

content.headline: End of Abyss makes survival horror feel like a tiny, dark diorama
content.shortHeadline: End of Abyss turns survival horror into a dollhouse
content.standfirst: This overhead horror game stages its monsters and ruined rooms like a miniature world, with clear echoes of Resident Evil and The Thing. The review praises its visual control but finds the extended backtracking draining.

image.caption: The small-scale world of End of Abyss.

sources.originalTitle: End of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing

segments.body: End of Abyss shrinks a decaying facility into a foggy, top-down world of carefully arranged rooms and bodies. The fixed perspective makes each scene feel like a diorama, allowing monsters to emerge from darkness just beyond the player’s attention. The review describes its best moments as compact, unsettling versions of classic survival-horror scares.

segments.title: When the map becomes a maze
segments.body: The game adds interconnected routes and exploration to its survival-horror foundations, but the reviewer finds the combination awkward. Slow movement, a confusing map and indistinct-looking rooms lead to repeated backtracking, and the staged scares lose their effect on repeated visits. The visual style remains strong even as the game outlasts its welcome.

content.headline: Replaying Modern Warfare 2 gave a father and son a new co-op story
content.shortHeadline: A father and son return to the game they first played together
content.standfirst: Seventeen years after they first tackled its co-op missions, a father and his grown son return to Modern Warfare 2. Their reunion becomes a story about teamwork, time and the pleasure of playing without pressure.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son revisit the Special Ops missions they began playing together when the boy was five. Their old habits remain: the father moves cautiously and scouts ahead, while his son charges in. After repeated failures, they find a compromise and finally complete missions they never managed as a child and parent.

segments.title: A shared memory in the making
segments.body: The game gives them a familiar reason to spend long evenings together, but the piece is less about mastery than about enjoying the time. The son tells his father he will remember the sessions as some of their best times; the writer reflects on the relief of playing without the usual pressures of work, parenthood and ambition.

content.headline: Blood antibody patterns may signal inflammatory bowel disease years early
content.shortHeadline: Blood signals may flag bowel disease years before diagnosis
content.standfirst: A study found immune patterns associated with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis in blood samples taken up to a decade before diagnosis. The findings are promising, but the researchers say this is not yet a clinical test.

image.caption: Research into blood antibody patterns could help identify people at risk of inflammatory bowel disease earlier.

sources.originalTitle: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

segments.body: Researchers examined 2,000 blood samples from 500 US military personnel, including people who later developed Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis. In those who went on to develop Crohn’s, antibodies to Epstein-Barr virus were more common; those who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies to a protein made by the body.

segments.title: A research lead, not a test
segments.body: Some antibody differences were visible as much as 10 years before diagnosis, and the signal was strongest in people who later developed more severe Crohn’s disease. The study shows an association, not that infection causes IBD, and the findings need confirmation in other groups. A gastroenterology professor not involved in the work called the techniques a research tool, not something ready for clinical use.

perspectives.body: The study’s lead author, Dr Arno Bourgonje, said the immune system may leave warning signs years before symptoms appear, but stressed that the results are not yet a test that can predict whether an individual will become ill.

content.headline: Four popular anti-ageing claims face a challenge from a longevity researcher
content.shortHeadline: A longevity researcher challenges four anti-ageing claims
content.standfirst: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that evidence behind claims about centenarians, “Blue Zones”, telomeres and young-blood treatments is weak or misleading. Some of his conclusions are contested, and the article is an expert’s critique, not a review of scientific consensus.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who criticises claims made in some anti-ageing research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Newman says records of extreme old age are often unreliable, making it hard to draw lessons from centenarians. He also challenges the evidence that so-called Blue Zones have unusually long-lived populations, arguing that the idea has been commercialised and rests on poor data. A company associated with the Blue Zones concept says its programmes are scientifically validated and that Newman’s work has been disproven.

segments.title: What the evidence does—and doesn’t—show
segments.body: Newman argues that telomeres, protective structures at chromosome ends, are not a simple route to extending life: later research has complicated early optimism about the theory.
