He also points to the lack of proven benefit and potential risks in young-plasma transfusions; the US Food and Drug Administration has warned that the practice has no proven clinical benefit for preventing ageing or memory loss.

perspectives.body: The article presents Newman’s sceptical assessment of several areas of longevity research. It also includes a response from a Blue Zones representative, who says Newman’s criticism has been disproven, and a 2015 paper cited by Nobel laureate Elizabeth Blackburn on telomere biology’s roles in human disease.

content.headline: UK review warns ADHD diagnoses may soon exceed population estimates in some
content.shortHeadline: UK review flags rising ADHD diagnoses and overdiagnosis risk
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says NHS diagnoses among some groups of young people are approaching or exceeding estimates of how common ADHD is. It warns of a possible shift towards overdiagnosis, but says current evidence does not prove it is happening at scale.

image.caption: The review examines rising rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses among young people.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: The review found that 5% of teenage boys had an ADHD diagnosis last year, up from 2% a decade earlier; among girls of the same age, the rate rose from 0.5% to 2.5%. It says diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism in some groups are approaching or already exceeding estimates of prevalence, while waiting lists continue to grow.

segments.title: A warning, not a verdict
segments.body: The authors say the figures do not establish that overdiagnosis is already occurring at scale. They point to challenges including subjective assessments, broader diagnostic definitions, greater awareness and incentives linked to support. The review’s lead author called the findings a warning sign, while other contributors say the balance of risks may be changing; underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis remain concerns too.

perspectives.body: Professor Peter Fonagy, who led the review’s authors, described the findings as a warning about overdiagnosis rather than a definitive conclusion that it is occurring.

content.headline: Light-activated gene therapy partially restores vision in a small study
content.shortHeadline: Light-activated gene therapy partly restored vision in six patients
content.standfirst: In a study of 10 people with severe vision loss from retinitis pigmentosa, six had meaningful improvement after treatment using a gene that makes retinal cells respond to amber light. The approach is experimental and did not restore normal sight.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control the activity of nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: The treatment introduces a gene into the retina so that some nerve cells respond to amber light. Patients wear glasses that convert ordinary light into amber shades. In the reported study, six of 10 participants had meaningful improvement after three months, including being able to pick up a cup from a table; they could not distinguish faces.

segments.title: A wider research prospect
segments.body: The approach is part of optogenetics, which uses light to control nerve cells. Researchers are also investigating possible applications in pain, epilepsy and hearing, but those uses remain at different stages of development. For hearing, for example, optogenetic implants have so far been tested in animals, and the gene therapy would need to be shown safe.

content.headline: Hotter, drier summers are prompting research into new UK food crops
content.shortHeadline: Could drought-tolerant crops reshape what UK growers plant?
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing crops such as lupins and chickpeas that may cope better with hotter, drier summers. They could broaden UK food production, but researchers say more work is needed on where varieties will grow and how pests and disease may affect them.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from a drought-tolerant crop being explored for future UK growing.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: A research group at Southampton is exploring crops that may be better suited to a changing climate. Lupin beans are drought-tolerant and can be milled into flour; chickpeas are already grown by a small number of UK farmers and may also cope with dry conditions. Researchers are working with chefs and food businesses to test possible uses.

segments.title: Adaptation has limits
segments.body: The researchers say they need to establish which varieties suit different parts of the UK and how pests and diseases could affect them before farmers plant them at scale. Warmer conditions may also help some crops while late spring frosts still threaten fruit blossom. The Royal Horticultural Society expects some growing patterns to shift north, but the winners and losers are not yet certain.

content.headline: Four European mobile carriers consider a joint bid for satellite phone service
content.shortHeadline: European carriers consider satellite service to rival Starlink
content.standfirst: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone say they are considering a joint bid for spectrum to support direct-to-device satellite service. They would build ground infrastructure, while a satellite partner has yet to be selected.

sources.originalTitle: Major European mobile carriers are teaming up for a ‘direct’ satellite program without Starlink

segments.body: The four operators have signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for spectrum that could support a European direct-to-device satellite service. They say it could extend coverage in underserved areas and strengthen the resilience of public networks. The companies would handle ground infrastructure, rather than investing directly in the satellite constellation.

The project still needs a satellite partner, which has not been announced, and the carriers say they are considering a bid rather than announcing a completed service. The plan follows a US collaboration among major mobile operators and comes as the EU considers reserving spectrum for local satellite services.

content.headline: Children as young as five are being targeted by online groomers, police warn
content.shortHeadline: Police warn online grooming is reaching children as young as five
content.standfirst: Police and child-safety groups say grooming is happening through social media, messaging and gaming platforms. Their advice to parents is to keep communication open and make clear that children can ask for help without blame.

image.caption: Police warn that children may be targeted through social media, messaging and gaming platforms.

sources.originalTitle: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'

segments.body: Avon and Somerset Police say children as young as five can be targeted online. The NSPCC recorded 756 sexual communication offences involving children in the South West in 2024–25, more than double the figure when the offence was introduced seven years ago. Snapchat was mentioned in 324 of the charity’s counselling sessions about online sexual abuse during 2025–26, followed by TikTok and Instagram.

segments.title: Keep a route to help open
segments.body: Police and the NSPCC advise parents to talk with children about their online lives and respond with warmth if a child discloses abuse. Police officer Andri Nicolau cautions against taking devices away or banning platforms, which could make children feel at fault. The NSPCC says children should know they have a trusted adult to turn to.

content.headline: Australian report calls for stronger privacy rules as employers use AI to track
content.shortHeadline: Australia urged to strengthen privacy rules for workplace monitoring
content.standfirst: A University of Technology Sydney institute says employers increasingly use tools including CCTV, keystroke tracking and AI systems to monitor workers, often without their knowledge. It wants workplace laws to require fairer, more transparent use.

image.caption: Workplace monitoring can include CCTV, tracking messages and monitoring workers’ computer activity.

sources.originalTitle: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff

segments.body: The Human Technology Institute says workplace monitoring is appearing across retail, offices, factories and delivery work. It cited a supermarket cashier who received a final written warning after an AI system flagged errors in about 0.18% of scans, and young fast-food workers who feared cameras were monitoring phone use in changing rooms.

segments.title: Proposed safeguards
segments.body: The institute wants workplace laws to require monitoring to be fair and reasonable, with employers consulting workers and explaining what data they collect. It also recommends a dedicated route for privacy complaints and powers to restrict surveillance products that pose unacceptable risks. A poll cited in the report found 43% of Australians knew some employers used monitoring technology, but only 9% knew it was used in their own workplace.

perspectives.body: The institute’s co-director, Edward Santow, said transparency is necessary but not sufficient, and called for a test of whether workplace monitoring is appropriate.

content.headline: AI coding tools are helping musicians rewrite the firmware in old gear
content.shortHeadline: AI is helping musicians unlock new features in old music gear
content.standfirst: Hobbyists are using coding assistants to build custom firmware for synthesizers, samplers and effects pedals, adding features that once required specialist skills. The projects can revive older equipment, but unofficial updates may contain bugs or damage devices.

sources.originalTitle: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down

segments.body: Musicians have used AI coding tools to add features to devices from brands including Elektron, Roland and Zoom. One community project has expanded the capabilities of Yamaha’s low-cost FM-1 synthesizer with new sound engines and sequencing options. Developers say coding assistants have made experiments possible in days that might once have taken weeks or months.

segments.title: The risks of unofficial updates
segments.body: Custom firmware is often less thoroughly tested than a manufacturer’s release and can cause devices to malfunction. Elektron warns that modifications can brick equipment or create problems when official software is updated. M-Vave, by contrast, has announced an open-source firmware and tools for its FM-1, signalling support for community development.

content.headline: Microsoft exits UK AI data-centre project after power supply delay
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft leaves UK AI data-centre project delayed until the 2030s
content.standfirst: Nscale says it remains committed to its planned £2bn site in Loughton, Essex, after Microsoft ended its involvement in funding a supercomputer there. The site’s power supply, expected by year-end, has reportedly been delayed until the 2030s.

image.caption: Nscale says it remains committed to its planned AI data centre in Loughton.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre

segments.body: The BBC understands Microsoft has terminated its involvement in the Loughton project, which Nscale announced last year. The company had said it would fund a supercomputer at the site. Nscale says it remains committed to the project and is exploring alternative power sources; Microsoft declined to comment to the BBC.

The data centre was due to receive power at the end of this year, but Nscale has been told that the supply will not arrive until the 2030s. The company says the delay does not affect its other contracts. The site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it opens, though the timing remains uncertain.

content.headline: Experts say AI could assist bioweapons work, but major barriers remain
content.shortHeadline: AI could help bioweapons work, but expertise and materials remain key
content.standfirst: Experts say AI tools could help people plan or troubleshoot biological weapons research, particularly by amplifying the work of skilled groups. But access to facilities, materials and practical know-how remains a substantial barrier.

sources.originalTitle: Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?

segments.body: The article examines how chatbots might help an unskilled person gather information or assist well-resourced researchers working with existing pathogens. Experts say the more immediate concern is that AI could amplify the capabilities of people who already have scientific expertise, rather than make bioweapons straightforward for anyone to produce.

segments.title: Information is not enough
segments.body: Scientists interviewed say dangerous work still requires access to biological materials and equipment, hands-on expertise, experimental validation and a way to scale and deliver a weapon. They also stress that biological research is often dual-use: work intended to improve disease prevention or treatment can raise security questions. The article says safeguards are uneven, with calls for independent model assessments and stronger screening of genetic-material orders.

perspectives.body: King’s College London’s Filippa Lentzos says AI does not remove the need for expertise, and that tacit knowledge, materials, equipment, validation, scale-up and delivery remain substantial barriers.

content.headline: Anthropic and Musk promise public-benefit share giveaways, but details are thin
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic and Musk promise large share donations, with details pending
content.standfirst: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund, while Elon Musk says he will give a SpaceX share to every US child. The mechanisms and conditions for Musk’s pledge have not been explained.

image.caption: Elon Musk announced plans to give a SpaceX share to every child in the United States.

sources.originalTitle: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
Musk and Anthropic pledge public share giveaways
Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
Musk and Anthropic pledge public share giveaways

segments.body: Anthropic says its fund will support public-benefit projects through donations to nonprofits or direct distributions. The company values the initial 5% commitment at about $48bn using its May valuation, subject to shareholder approval; it says another 2% could be added for each 50% rise in its value above an undisclosed baseline. Governance details are still to come.

segments.title: Musk’s pledge is not yet specified
segments.body: Musk said he would give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year, a promise valued by TechCrunch at more than $10bn using the current share price. It is unclear how the shares would be distributed. The announcements arrive amid scrutiny of AI’s effects on jobs and society, and as Anthropic prepares for a possible stock-market listing.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reports that Musk has not explained how the shares would reach children, and notes that his past charitable giving has largely gone through his own foundation.

content.headline: Teen accounts accessed 135 apps with AI nudification features, report finds
content.shortHeadline: Report finds teens could access 135 apps with nudification features
content.standfirst: Researchers using test accounts registered to 13-year-olds downloaded 135 apps with features that could generate nonconsensual nude imagery. The findings expose gaps in app-store age ratings and parental controls; Apple says it has tightened its rules.

image.caption: A report found that some apps with AI nudification features remained accessible to teen accounts.

sources.originalTitle: US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds
Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review

segments.body: The Tech Transparency Project created test accounts for 13-year-olds and found that they could download 135 apps with features to digitally undress people or place faces on nude bodies. Researchers used AI-generated images in their tests, not photographs of real women. Some apps were rated suitable for young users despite features the researchers said could be used to create sexual imagery.

segments.title: App-store controls under scrutiny
segments.body: Apple said it reviewed the findings, took action on apps identified in the report and strengthened its guidelines to require developers to prevent and remove nonconsensual intimate imagery. It says apps that conceal harmful features until after review are prohibited. Google said it regularly acts against harmful content and had suspended violating apps and restricted related search terms.

perspectives.body: Apple says its revised rules prohibit apps that hide harmful features, including nudification, until after app review, and that it can remove apps and developers that misrepresent their products.

content.headline: AI-assisted impersonation is putting freelance journalists’ reputations at risk
content.shortHeadline: AI-assisted impostors are using journalists’ names to pitch stories
content.standfirst: Two journalists say impostors used their names to pitch editors, and one bogus article appeared under a real writer’s byline. The cases may be linked, but who is behind the accounts—and whether AI was used in every instance—remains unknown.

image.caption: Journalist Linda Geddes says someone used her name to pitch stories and publish work under her byline.

sources.originalTitle: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Linda Geddes says someone used her name to pitch publications and attach her byline to a New York Post article. Caroline Williams discovered that Science had published a paid article under her name that she says she did not write; the journal later removed it after identifying copied quotes and a draft its software flagged as AI-written. Editors told the i Paper that the writer had presented themselves as the UK journalist.

segments.title: Linked clues, no confirmed culprit
segments.body: Geddes and Williams found clues suggesting a connection between impersonation attempts, but the identity and motive of the person or people involved are unresolved. The account contacted by the i Paper denied impersonating Williams and said the Science article was its own work, but declined a video call. Editors say they are increasing checks on new contributors; experts recommend verifying unusual approaches through independently confirmed contact details.

perspectives.body: The person contacted by the i Paper denied impersonating Caroline Williams and said the Science article was their own work, while declining an offer of a video call. Science’s managing news editor said the pitch had clearly identified itself as the UK journalist.

content.headline: AI agents reportedly used to break into more than 100 websites
content.shortHeadline: AI agents helped a hacker breach more than 100 websites, report says
content.standfirst: A security firm says a hacker used largely autonomous agents to attack more than 100 sites, including properties linked to John Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. The companies’ responses differ, and the extent of any sensitive-data access is not established.

sources.originalTitle: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents

segments.body: Norforge says it found exposed activity from Cairn, an open-source platform that can coordinate AI agents. Reuters reported that one user set out preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters and that successful breaches took about 23 hours. Norforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances it considered likely malicious.

segments.title: What the companies say
segments.body: John Deere said it had no indication that sensitive information was accessed. Cummins said it was investigating a potential attack on a third-party vendor’s site, while SharkNinja said a standalone site containing product-support information was affected and the threat had been contained. Norforge says it is working to take down malicious instances; Cairn’s creator says misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the platform.

perspectives.body: John Deere said it had no indication that sensitive information was accessed; SharkNinja said the affected site held product-support information and that it had contained the threat.

content.headline: Democrats see AI oversight as a possible political opening before midterms
content.shortHeadline: Democrats look to make AI regulation a campaign issue
content.standfirst: With voters concerned about jobs, data centres and online safety, Democratic strategists see an opportunity to challenge Republicans’ opposition to broad AI regulation. What oversight would look like remains unsettled, and the party has yet to agree on a detailed agenda.

sources.originalTitle: Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge

segments.body: Democratic strategists say public concern about AI could help the party press for closer scrutiny if it wins control of a chamber of Congress. They point to issues including data-centre impacts, job displacement and safety checks on advanced models. Campaign ads are already linking AI policy to questions about children’s safety and who bears the costs of new infrastructure.

segments.title: Policy lines remain open
segments.body: Possible proposals discussed include independent researchers working with frontier AI labs, more safety checks and greater company liability for harms. But lawmakers have not reached broad agreement, and AI is not yet a leading issue driving voters to the polls. The article’s strategists argue Democrats need a compelling message, while acknowledging that the direction and intensity of oversight are still undecided.

perspectives.body: Democratic strategist Jesse Lehrich says AI is a political opportunity, but questions whether Democrats are willing and able to seize it; the article notes that congressional proposals have not yet gained broad consensus.

content.headline: Meta removes terms that raised concerns about scraping content to train AI
content.shortHeadline: Meta removes disputed terms on crawling business websites
content.standfirst: Meta removed language from its commercial terms that legal experts said might allow it to use material from associated websites to develop or train AI. The company says the terms applied to advertising and business products and did not change its crawling practices.

sources.originalTitle: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns

segments.body: The wording had appeared to let Meta use content from websites associated with business accounts to develop, research or train its products. Legal experts cited in earlier coverage said it could be read as overriding site owners’ instructions against crawling. After criticism, Meta removed the language and clarified its terms.

segments.title: Meta’s explanation
segments.body: Meta says the consolidated crawling terms applied only to advertising and business products, did not give it new rights and did not change how its web crawlers work. The change is not evidence that Meta had scraped publishers’ sites under the disputed wording; the reporting documents a concern about what the terms could be read to permit.

perspectives.body: Meta said the terms applied only to its ads and business products, and that content owners can still use robots.txt to signal their preferences.

content.headline: AI is making familiar scams more convincing, trading standards officers warn
content.shortHeadline: AI makes fake shops and impersonation scams harder to spot
content.standfirst: Trading standards officers warn that AI can help criminals make polished fake retail sites, personalised phishing messages and convincing voice or video impersonations. They say spelling mistakes are no longer a reliable warning sign.

sources.originalTitle: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

segments.body: National Trading Standards has issued its first AI scam watchlist, describing how criminals can create fake retailer websites, maintain romance scams with personalised messages and imitate friends or relatives using cloned voices or deepfake video. The group says AI can also generate phishing messages at scale and make them appear error-free.

segments.title: Pause and verify
segments.body: Trading standards advises checking a business’s address and contacting it through independently verified details. Do not assume someone is genuine because you recognise their voice or see them on a video call, and be wary of pressure to act quickly. The guidance says not to send money or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person.
